text: 1 Research note

title: National Survey on Cancer Prevention Awareness and Practice 2025
text:
1.1 Literature review
(Choi, Oh, et al. 2025)

The Korean Code Against Cancer comprises a set of recommendations intended to prevent cancer.
The National Cancer Control Committee approved the currently published 10 codes for cancer prevention.

no smoking and avoidance of secondhand smoke;
consuming sufficient fruits and vegetables as part of a balanced diet;
reducing salt intake and avoiding burnt or charred foods;
limiting alcohol consumption;
engaging in regular physical activity (at least 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week);
maintaining a healthy body weight;
receiving immunization against hepatitis B virus and human papillomavirus;
practicing safe sex by maintaining a single sexual partner and using condoms;
following health and safety guidelines to avoid exposure to occupational carcinogens;
undergoing regular cancer screening



1.1.1 Related works
(Oh et al. 2022)

reports data regarding the awareness and practice of cancer prevention among Koreans in 2021 and behavioral changes during the coronavirus disease 2019
evaluated their associations with potential risk factors through multiple logistic regression analysis adjusted for age, gender, residence, marital status, education, and income.

Finding:

80% aware, 45% practice. Characteristics among
The level of awareness and practice regarding cancer prevention has not changed significantly over the last 15 years, even though various campaigns and social events to raise awareness have been conducted.

=> Overall of the awareness and practice of 10 codes from 2007 to 2021
(Choi, Kim, et al. 2025)

This study found that while awareness was reasonably high among both men and women, there was a significant gender gap in practice

=> access the awareness and practice of 10 codes among 2 groups (men and women) from 2007 to 2023
(Kwon et al. 2025)

mediation analysis: knowledge(exposure), attidude (mediator), practice (outcome) between 2014 and 2023 to assess both the direct and indirect effects of these variables on smoking behavior
only consider in ex-smoker and current-smoker

Finding:

Knowledge that smoking causes cancer was associated with a higher likelihood of having a positive attitude toward quitting smoking to prevent cancer
Knowledge was associated with a higher likelihood of practicing smoking cessation
Attitude was also associated with a higher likelihood of practicing smoking cessation
KAP model: attitude toward smoking cessation for cancer prevention mediated the relationship between knowledge of smoking’s role in causing cancer and the practice of smoking cessation
Prioritizing the identification of factors that influence smoking cessation behaviors is essential for the development and implementation of effective policies, as these factors may serve as mediating variables in smoking cessation practices

=> health education programs could effectively promote better attitudes and support healthy behaviors

Based on these findings, if current tobacco control policies have predominantly focused on “cigarettes” and reducing tobacco consumption among smokers, future policies should pivot toward “comprehensive regulation” and smoking prevention, emphasizing the importance of “attitudes” and “knowledge” among both smokers and non-smokers

Research limitation:

future investigations should incorporate gender analyses
future research should also include individuals affected by secondhand and thirdhand smoke

(Choi, Jung, and Kim 2025)

Surveyed Korean adults to identify the awareness and practice of the recommended guidelines for dietary factors.

(Nguyen et al. 2025)

Identify the factors influencing PCa screening behavior and explore the underlying motivations among Korean men

title: National Survey on Cancer Prevention Awareness and Practice 2025
section: 1.3 Smoking-related knowledge, attitude, and practice for cancer prevention
text:
1.3 Smoking-related knowledge, attitude, and practice for cancer prevention

Knowlegde:

Evaluated by assessing whether individuals were aware of the no-smoking guidelines and whether they understood that smoking causes cancer

Awareness:

The following questions were posed:
“Do you think smoking causes cancer?”
“Do you think that not smoking (i.e., avoiding smoking and secondhand smoke) prevents cancer?”
=> Knowledge of the link between smoking and cancer was determined by considering only those respondents who answered “yes” to these questions

Attitude:

Assessed by asking “Do you think about the recommendation to quit smoking for cancer prevention?” with the following response categories: “I do not think about it,” “I have not decided to quit smoking yet,” “I do not try to quit smoking,” and “I will quit smoking.”
=> positive attitude toward smoking cessation was operationally defined as responding “I will quit smoking.”

Practice:

Assessed by asking, “Have you ever smoked?” with the following response categories: “non-smoker,” “ex-smoker,” and “current smoker.”
This study included only individuals with a history of smoking, thereby excluding those who had never smoked.

Q2_1: National cancer prevention support (Cancer prevention projects such as smoking cessation, sobriety, diet, HPV vaccination, etc.)
